questions.why: Reliability under failure is the core of mobile design.
questions.mistake: Sending directly from the screen with no local record or idempotency key.
questions.followUp: How would you order messages from two devices?

questions.text: Why use cursor pagination for a feed?
questions.answer: New posts arriving at the top shift offsets and cause duplicates or gaps; a cursor points at a specific item, so pages stay stable.
questions.why: It tests data consistency in a very common feature.
questions.mistake: Giving offset pagination with a larger page size as the fix.
questions.followUp: How does the server build the next cursor?

questions.text: REST, GraphQL or gRPC for a mobile app?
questions.answer: REST is simple and cacheable; GraphQL fetches exactly what each screen needs in one request; gRPC is compact and fast with streaming but harder to debug. Choose based on the team and backend.
questions.why: They want trade-offs tied to a context.
questions.mistake: Naming a favourite without asking about the clients and backend.
questions.followUp: When would you add a backend-for-frontend?

questions.text: How would you resolve conflicts when two devices edit the same note offline?
questions.answer: Give each record a version and timestamps, sync through an outbox, and use a clear rule, such as last-write-wins per field, keeping a conflict copy when both changed the same field so no data is lost.
questions.why: Conflict handling shows whether you've thought about data loss.
questions.mistake: Applying last-write-wins to the whole record and silently losing edits.
questions.followUp: When would you use CRDTs?

questions.text: How would you design an app that 10 teams contribute to?
questions.answer: Feature modules owned by teams, a shared design system, clear module contracts, convention plugins, code owners, feature flags, a release train and per-module CI.
questions.why: It probes whether you can design for organisations, not only code.
questions.mistake: Talking only about folder structure.
questions.followUp: How do you keep app startup fast with so many teams?

questions.text: How do you keep real-time updates battery-friendly?
questions.answer: Keep a WebSocket only while the app is in the foreground, use push messages to trigger syncs in the background, and reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter.
questions.why: It tests whether you weigh freshness against battery and data use.
questions.mistake: Keeping a socket open in the background or polling every few seconds.
questions.followUp: How would you handle messages missed while disconnected?

questions.text: How do you design reliable background photo or video uploads on mobile?
questions.answer: Persist the job in Room, compress off the main thread into `cacheDir`, run the upload in WorkManager with network constraints, and use chunked resumable uploads so retries don't restart from zero.
questions.why: Media uploads combine memory limits, WorkManager, and resumable networking.
questions.mistake: Uploading inside `viewModelScope` or reading the whole file into memory.
questions.followUp: How do you avoid uploading a 12-megapixel raw photo over cellular?

questions.text: What changes when your app targets Android 17 on a tablet?
questions.answer: The app can no longer opt out of orientation and resizability restrictions on large screens (games excepted), so layouts must adapt to any window size and survive resizing without losing state.
questions.why: Large-screen requirements affect apps that assumed portrait phones.
questions.mistake: Assuming a locked orientation will still be honoured everywhere.
questions.followUp: Which layouts break first on a large window?

questions.text: How do you make an app edge-to-edge safely?
questions.answer: Call `enableEdgeToEdge()`, let `Scaffold` or `WindowInsets.safeDrawing` pad content, use `imePadding()` for input, and test with gesture and 3-button navigation, cutouts and the keyboard.
questions.why: Recent Android versions make this unavoidable.
questions.mistake: Adding fixed padding in dp to avoid the system bars.
questions.followUp: How do you handle the keyboard inset in a list?

questions.text: Why does predictive back require changing how you handle back?
questions.answer: The system must know before the gesture ends whether the app will intercept it, so you register callbacks and enable them only when needed, instead of deciding in `onBackPressed()`.
questions.why: It checks that you know why the old back callback no longer fits.
questions.mistake: Intercepting back all the time, even when there's nothing to handle.
questions.followUp: How do you animate with the back gesture?

questions.text: Why use window size classes instead of checking for a tablet?
questions.answer: A tablet in split-screen can be compact and a foldable changes size; the window size is what the layout actually has.
questions.why: To see that you design for window sizes rather than device types.
questions.mistake: Reading the physical screen size or checking for "tablet".
questions.followUp: What are the window width size classes?

questions.text: What would you share first in a KMP project?
questions.answer: Networking, models, persistence and business logic in one module. Keep UI native at first, measure the build and binary-size impact, and involve the iOS team early.
questions.why: They're looking for a realistic, low-risk adoption plan.
questions.mistake: Proposing to share all UI and logic from the first day.
questions.followUp: What would you not share?

questions.text: How do you test accessibility?
questions.answer: TalkBack walk-throughs of key journeys, Accessibility Scanner, automated checks in UI tests, large font and display sizes, and contrast checks in design review.
questions.why: Accessibility is a quality requirement and often a legal one.
questions.mistake: Relying only on an automated scanner.
questions.followUp: Which automated accessibility checks can run in CI?

questions.text: Why is `"$count items"` a localization bug?
questions.answer: Many languages have several plural forms and different word order. Use `<plurals>` with `pluralStringResource` or `getQuantityString`, and positional arguments.
questions.why: It shows whether you've shipped to more than one language.
questions.mistake: Handling plurals with an `if` for count equals one.
questions.followUp: How do you handle right-to-left languages?

questions.text: When would you use on-device AI instead of a server model?
questions.answer: When privacy, latency or offline use matters and the task fits a small model; check device support and keep a server fallback.
questions.why: They want you to weigh privacy, latency, cost and device support.
questions.mistake: Assuming every device can run the model.
questions.followUp: What is your fallback if the model is unavailable?

questions.text: How do you handle foldable hinges and postures in an adaptive UI?
questions.answer: Read `FoldingFeature` via `WindowInfoTracker` or `currentWindowAdaptiveInfo().windowPosture` to split panes cleanly around the hinge bounds and adapt to tabletop or book postures.
questions.why: Foldables introduce split-pane boundaries and postures that standard responsive breakpoints miss.
questions.mistake: Letting dialogs or buttons render directly across the physical hinge.
questions.followUp: What is the difference between tabletop and book posture?

questions.text: How do you prevent a phone layout from looking stretched on a tablet or desktop window?
questions.answer: Constrain readable content with `widthIn(max = 600.dp)` or multi-column grids, and switch to `ListDetailPaneScaffold` or `SupportingPaneScaffold` at `Expanded` (`>= 840 dp`) width.
questions.why: Resizing a phone layout without max-width constraints or multi-pane scaffolds hurts usability.
questions.mistake: Using `fillMaxWidth()` everywhere without bounding line length or adding a secondary pane.
questions.followUp: Which Material 3 adaptive scaffold fits a feed-plus-reader screen?

questions.text: Tell me about a technical decision others disagreed with.
questions.answer: Show how you gathered data, listened, wrote it up or prototyped, and either persuaded the team or committed to their choice with a checkpoint.
questions.why: They want evidence that you can influence others and handle disagreement.
questions.mistake: Telling a story where you were simply right and others eventually saw it.
questions.followUp: What would you do differently next time?

questions.text: Describe a production incident you caused.
questions.answer: Own it, explain the fix for users, the blameless post-mortem, and the process change that prevents a repeat.
questions.why: It tests ownership and what you learned.
questions.mistake: Blaming someone else or picking a trivial incident.
questions.followUp: How did you make sure it didn't happen again?

questions.text: How do you mentor junior developers?
questions.answer: Give one specific person and outcome: pairing, gradually larger tasks, review feedback that teaches, and their growth as the result.
questions.why: Senior engineers are expected to raise the team's level.
questions.mistake: Describing mentoring in general terms, with no person or outcome.
questions.followUp: How did you know the mentoring worked?

questions.text: How do you handle tech debt?
questions.answer: Measure its cost, link it to business impact, fix it incrementally with reserved capacity, and avoid big-bang rewrites.
questions.why: To see whether you connect engineering work to business impact.
questions.mistake: Asking for a rewrite because the code is ugly.
questions.followUp: How did you get time for the work?

questions.text: How do you do code reviews?
questions.answer: Review quickly, automate style, focus on correctness, design and tests, explain the why, and separate must-fix comments from suggestions.
questions.why: Reviews show how you work with other people.
questions.mistake: Focusing on style nits that tools should catch.
questions.followUp: How do you handle a disagreement in a review?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you pushed back on product.
questions.answer: Explain the risk in user and business terms, offer an alternative such as a smaller first version, and agree on a decision together.
questions.why: They're checking how you handle conflict with non-engineers.
questions.mistake: Either refusing outright or agreeing and quietly missing the date.
questions.followUp: What did you learn about the product side?

questions.text: What makes a developer senior rather than mid-level?
questions.answer: Scope beyond their own tasks, sound trade-off decisions, raising the team's level through mentoring and standards, and owning outcomes in production.
questions.why: It reveals how you see your own responsibility.
questions.mistake: Answering with years of experience or a list of technologies.
questions.followUp: Give an example from your own work.

questions.text: Implement an LRU cache with O(1) operations.
questions.answer: Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list; move nodes to the front on access and evict from the tail when over capacity. In production, `LinkedHashMap` with access order or `LruCache`.
questions.why: It tests data structure choice under complexity constraints.
questions.mistake: Using only a list, which makes lookups or moves O(n).
questions.followUp: How would you make it thread-safe?

questions.text: Find two numbers that add up to a target.
questions.answer: One pass with a map of seen values to indices, checking for the complement: O(n) time and space.
questions.why: A warm-up that checks you can trade memory for speed.
questions.mistake: Stopping at the nested-loop O(n^2) solution.
questions.followUp: What changes if the array is already sorted?

questions.text: Longest substring without repeating characters?
questions.answer: Sliding window with the last index of each character; move the left edge past repeats. O(n).
questions.why: It tests the sliding window technique.
questions.mistake: Restarting the window from scratch after every repeat.
questions.followUp: What changes if you need the substring itself?

questions.text: Count islands in a grid.
questions.answer: BFS or DFS from each unvisited land cell, marking the island as visited. O(rows times columns).
questions.why: It checks grid traversal and visited tracking.
questions.mistake: Forgetting to mark cells visited, which loops or counts an island twice.
questions.followUp: How would you solve it without changing the grid?

questions.text: Top K frequent elements?
questions.answer: Count with a map, keep a min-heap of size k: O(n log k); bucket sort gives O(n).
questions.why: It tests knowing when sorting everything is unnecessary.
questions.mistake: Sorting all items without discussing a heap or buckets.
questions.followUp: What if the data is a stream?

questions.text: Write a debounce function with coroutines.
questions.answer: Keep the last job, cancel it on each call, and launch a new one that delays and then runs the action.
questions.why: It shows whether you can use cancellation correctly.
questions.mistake: Using threads or timers and never cancelling the earlier job.
questions.followUp: How would you write a throttle instead?

questions.text: Run 100 downloads, at most 4 at a time.
questions.answer: `async` for each item inside `coroutineScope`, with a `Semaphore(4)` and `withPermit` around the work, then `awaitAll`.
questions.why: It tests bounded concurrency with structured coroutines.
questions.mistake: Launching all 100 at once, or processing them one at a time.
questions.followUp: How do you handle one failed download without cancelling the rest?

questions.text: What's wrong with `catch (e: Exception)` inside a coroutine?
questions.answer: It also catches `CancellationException`, so the coroutine ignores cancellation. Rethrow it or catch specific exceptions.
questions.why: A small snippet that exposes cancellation bugs.
questions.mistake: Saying it's fine because the error is logged.
questions.followUp: How would you write this so it never swallows cancellation?

questions.text: What do you put in a take-home README?
questions.answer: How to run it, the architecture and why, trade-offs and shortcuts, and what you'd improve with more time.
questions.why: Reviewers judge how clearly you explain your decisions.
questions.mistake: Listing only run instructions and no trade-offs.
questions.followUp: What would you build next, and why?

questions.text: How do you merge overlapping intervals?
questions.answer: Sort by start time, then walk once: append non-overlapping intervals and extend the last end with `maxOf` when they overlap. O(n log n) time.
questions.why: It tests sorting plus a clean single-pass invariant.
questions.mistake: Forgetting to take `maxOf` on the end bound when one interval contains another.
questions.followUp: How would you insert one new interval into an already sorted list?

questions.text: How would you implement a sliding-window rate limiter in Kotlin?
questions.answer: Store an `ArrayDeque<Long>` of timestamps per key with an injected clock, evict entries older than `now - windowMs`, and allow the call only if `size < maxRequests`.
questions.why: Rate limiting tests queue eviction, concurrency safety, and testable time.
questions.mistake: Hardcoding `System.currentTimeMillis()` so tests have to sleep.
questions.followUp: When would you switch to a token bucket?

questions.text: How do you order tasks or initializers that have dependencies?
questions.answer: Use topological sort (Kahn's algorithm): track in-degrees, start a queue with in-degree 0 nodes, decrement neighbours as you pop, and flag a cycle if fewer than all nodes are output.
questions.why: Topological sort shows up in build graphs, App Startup initializers, and task runners.
questions.mistake: Not checking whether a cycle prevented all nodes from being scheduled.
questions.followUp: How would you run independent tasks in parallel?

questions.text: How do you build and test an in-memory cache with a TTL?
questions.answer: Store values with an `expiresAt` timestamp in a bounded `LinkedHashMap`, evict expired entries on `get`, and inject a clock lambda so unit tests can advance time deterministically.
questions.why: TTL caches are a practical Android pattern for config and search results.
questions.mistake: Leaving the cache size unbounded or sleeping in unit tests.
questions.followUp: Should the clock use wall-clock time or `elapsedRealtime`?

questions.text: `val` vs `const val`?
questions.answer: `val` is read-only and set at runtime; `const val` is a compile-time constant that gets inlined, and only works for primitives and String
questions.why: A fast check of Kotlin basics.
questions.mistake: Saying they're interchangeable.
questions.followUp: Where can you declare a `const val`?

questions.text: `lateinit` on an `Int`?
questions.answer: Not allowed, because primitives can't be null internally; use `Delegates.notNull()` or a nullable type
questions.why: It checks that you know where `lateinit` can't be used.
questions.mistake: Trying `lateinit var count: Int`.
questions.followUp: How do you check whether a `lateinit` property is set?

questions.answer: `==` compares content using `equals`; `===` checks it's the same object
questions.why: Equality mistakes cause subtle bugs.
questions.mistake: Assuming `==` compares references, as it does for Java objects.
questions.followUp: When do two data class instances satisfy `==`?

questions.text: `Any`, `Unit` and `Nothing`?
questions.answer: `Any` is the root type; `Unit` means "no useful result"; `Nothing` means "never returns", like `throw`
questions.why: These types appear throughout Kotlin signatures.
questions.mistake: Treating `Nothing` and `Unit` as the same.
questions.followUp: Where does the compiler use `Nothing`?

questions.text: What is a `suspend` function under the hood?
questions.answer: The compiler adds a `Continuation` parameter and turns the body into a state machine that can pause and resume
questions.why: A short probe of whether you understand suspension.
questions.mistake: Saying it always runs on a background thread.
questions.followUp: What is a continuation?

questions.text: `Job` vs `SupervisorJob`?
questions.answer: With `Job`, a child's failure cancels the parent and siblings; with `SupervisorJob`, children fail independently
questions.why: Failure handling is a frequent follow-up.
questions.mistake: Thinking a supervisor catches the exception for you.
questions.followUp: Where have you used a `SupervisorJob`?

questions.text: `coroutineScope` vs `supervisorScope`?
questions.answer: The same difference, as suspending functions: one failure cancels all, or each child fails alone
questions.why: It checks that you can apply supervision inside a suspend function.
questions.mistake: Expecting `supervisorScope` to ignore a failure in its own body.
questions.followUp: What happens to the exception in each?

questions.text: `StateFlow` vs `SharedFlow`?
questions.answer: `StateFlow` always has a current value and skips equal values; `SharedFlow` has no initial value and configurable replay, good for events
questions.why: Using the wrong one loses or repeats events.
questions.mistake: Treating `StateFlow` as an event stream.
questions.followUp: How do you configure replay?

questions.text: Cold vs hot Flow?
questions.answer: A cold flow starts fresh for each collector; a hot flow runs whether or not anyone collects
questions.why: It underpins how you reason about Flow work.
questions.mistake: Assuming a cold flow shares one execution between collectors.
questions.followUp: How do you turn a cold flow into a hot one?

questions.text: When do you use `flatMapLatest`?
questions.answer: Search as you type: a new query cancels the previous search
questions.why: It checks that you can match an operator to a use case.
questions.mistake: Using it for work that must not be cancelled, such as saving.
questions.followUp: How is it different from `collectLatest`?

questions.text: `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` vs `collectAsState`?
questions.answer: The lifecycle version stops collecting when the app goes to the background
questions.why: It shows lifecycle awareness in Compose.
questions.mistake: Using `collectAsState` for flows that do expensive work.
questions.followUp: Why does the difference matter for battery?

questions.text: What is `derivedStateOf` for?
questions.answer: State computed from other state that changes less often than its inputs, so it avoids extra recompositions
questions.why: It tests targeted performance knowledge.
questions.mistake: Using it simply to combine two values.
questions.followUp: When is it the wrong tool?

questions.text: What makes a type stable in Compose?
questions.answer: It's immutable, or it tells Compose when it changes; all public properties are `val` and stable themselves
questions.why: Stability explains many recomposition questions.
questions.mistake: Thinking `val` alone makes a type stable.
questions.followUp: What does `@Immutable` promise?

questions.text: Does a ViewModel survive process death?
questions.answer: No; use `SavedStateHandle` for small UI state and a database for real data
questions.why: It checks the most common ViewModel misunderstanding.
questions.mistake: Answering yes because it survives rotation.
questions.followUp: How do you restore state after it?

questions.text: What limits the size of a saved-state Bundle?
questions.answer: The Binder transaction buffer, about 1 MB shared by the process, so keep saved state small
questions.why: A limit behind real crashes.
questions.mistake: Assuming the whole 1 MB is available to one screen.
questions.followUp: How would you find a transaction that is too large?

questions.text: `Serializable` vs `Parcelable`?
questions.answer: `Serializable` uses reflection and is slow; `Parcelable` is explicit and fast, and `@Parcelize` writes it for you
questions.why: A quick IPC basics check.
questions.mistake: Saying there's no difference on Android.
questions.followUp: What does `@Parcelize` generate?

questions.text: LiveData `setValue` vs `postValue`?
questions.answer: `setValue` runs on the main thread immediately; `postValue` works from any thread but can drop intermediate values
questions.why: It catches lost updates in older codebases.
questions.mistake: Expecting every `postValue` to be delivered.
questions.followUp: Which should a background thread use?

questions.text: SharedPreferences `commit()` vs `apply()`?
questions.answer: `commit()` writes synchronously and returns success; `apply()` writes in the background but can still block at lifecycle points, a common ANR cause
questions.why: It connects storage APIs to ANRs.
questions.mistake: Believing `apply()` can never block the main thread.
questions.followUp: When would you use DataStore instead?

questions.text: `Service` vs WorkManager?
questions.answer: A `Service` runs on the main thread and you manage its work and lifetime; WorkManager is for deferrable work that must be guaranteed; `IntentService` is deprecated
questions.why: To check you pick modern background tools.
questions.mistake: Still proposing `IntentService`.
questions.followUp: When do you need a foreground service?

questions.text: `Dispatchers.IO` vs `Default`?
questions.answer: `IO` is for blocking I/O and has many threads; `Default` is for CPU work and has one thread per core
questions.why: Choosing wrongly can starve threads.
questions.mistake: Running blocking I/O on `Default`.
questions.followUp: How would you inject dispatchers for tests?

questions.text: What are the ANR thresholds?
questions.answer: About 5 seconds for input and about 10 seconds for a foreground broadcast receiver
questions.why: A quick check of ANR knowledge.
questions.mistake: Giving one number for every kind of ANR.
questions.followUp: What does the system do when one happens?

questions.text: What does R8 do?
questions.answer: It shrinks, obfuscates and optimises code; anything used by reflection needs keep rules
questions.why: It checks release-build basics.
questions.mistake: Saying it only obfuscates.
questions.followUp: When do you need a keep rule?

questions.text: `@Binds` vs `@Provides`?
questions.answer: `@Binds` maps an interface to an implementation with no code; `@Provides` is a function you write to build the object
questions.why: A standard Dagger and Hilt check.
questions.mistake: Swapping the two.
questions.followUp: When must you use `@Provides`?

questions.text: Hilt scope for an object shared only within one screen's ViewModel?
questions.answer: `@ViewModelScoped`
questions.why: It tests precise scoping.
questions.mistake: Choosing `@Singleton` for screen-only state.
questions.followUp: Which component does that scope live in?

questions.text: Why must `exported` be declared?
questions.answer: Since Android 12, components with intent filters must say whether other apps can start them, for security
questions.why: A platform security change you should know.
questions.mistake: Setting every component to exported.
questions.followUp: Which components need it?

questions.text: `PendingIntent` mutability flag?
questions.answer: Required since Android 12; prefer `FLAG_IMMUTABLE` unless something must fill in the intent
questions.why: It's a required security decision.
questions.mistake: Defaulting to mutable.
questions.followUp: When would `FLAG_MUTABLE` be needed?

questions.text: Why did libraries use a `ContentProvider`?
questions.answer: To initialise automatically at app start, now replaced by App Startup; providers also share data through URIs
questions.why: It shows you understand some history behind app startup.
questions.mistake: Adding more providers for initialisation today.
questions.followUp: What does App Startup change?

questions.text: What does `Looper.prepare()` do?
questions.answer: It creates a message loop for the current thread, which is how `HandlerThread` works
questions.why: It probes how Android's main thread machinery works.
questions.mistake: Thinking every thread already has a looper.
questions.followUp: Which threads already have a Looper?

questions.text: What is Doze?
questions.answer: An idle mode that delays network, jobs and alarms to short maintenance windows to save battery
questions.why: It checks power management basics.
questions.mistake: Assuming alarms and jobs always fire on time.
questions.followUp: How do you test behaviour in Doze?

questions.text: Why does the 16 KB page size matter?
questions.answer: Newer devices use 16 KB memory pages, so native libraries must be rebuilt and aligned for it
questions.why: It checks awareness of a recent compatibility requirement.
questions.mistake: Thinking pure Kotlin or Java apps need native rebuilds.
questions.followUp: How do you check a native library's alignment?

questions.text: Companion object vs top-level function?
questions.answer: A companion is a real object inside the class, good for factories and private access; top-level functions are simpler for plain utilities
questions.why: A Kotlin design basics check.
questions.mistake: Putting every utility in a companion object.
questions.followUp: When does a companion object implement an interface?

questions.text: `let` vs `apply`?
questions.answer: `let` passes the object as `it` and returns the lambda result; `apply` uses `this` and returns the object, good for configuring
questions.why: A quick scope function check.
questions.mistake: Mixing up what each returns.
questions.followUp: When would you use `also` instead?

questions.text: What is a GC root, and how does it relate to memory leaks?
questions.answer: A starting point the collector treats as always alive: static fields, live threads' local variables, JNI references. A leak is an unneeded object still reachable from a root, such as an Activity in a static field.
questions.why: It tests whether you can explain leaks from first principles.
questions.mistake: Saying anything with a reference to it is leaked.
questions.followUp: Is an object referenced only by a dead object a leak?

questions.text: When would you use `WeakReference`?
questions.answer: When a longer-lived object must point at an Activity or View without keeping it alive. Prefer proper unregistration or lifecycle-aware flows; a weak reference is a fallback.
questions.why: They want to know if you see it as a fallback, not a fix.
questions.mistake: Wrapping references in `WeakReference` instead of unregistering them.
questions.followUp: How is `SoftReference` different?

questions.text: Is `@Volatile var count` enough for a thread-safe counter?
questions.answer: No. It gives visibility, but `count++` is read-modify-write and can lose updates. Use `AtomicInteger`, a lock, a `Mutex`, or keep it on one thread.
questions.why: It exposes confusion between visibility and atomicity.
questions.mistake: Saying volatile makes `count++` thread-safe.
questions.followUp: When is `synchronized` still the right tool?

questions.text: Why does double-checked locking need `@Volatile`?
questions.answer: Without it, another thread can see the reference before the constructor finishes and use a half-built object. `@Volatile` adds the happens-before guarantee.
questions.why: A classic test of the memory model.
questions.mistake: Saying the lock alone is enough.
questions.followUp: Why is a Kotlin `object` or `lazy` simpler?

questions.text: How do you avoid deadlocks?
questions.answer: Take locks in a fixed order, keep critical sections short, don't call external code while holding a lock, and prefer immutable data, thread confinement or a coroutine `Mutex`.
questions.why: It shows practical concurrency experience.
questions.mistake: Adding more locks without a fixed order.
questions.followUp: How would you detect a deadlock?

questions.text: Why are coroutines cheaper than threads?
questions.answer: A suspended coroutine gives its thread back, so thousands share a small pool, while each thread needs its own stack of about a megabyte.
questions.why: To check the mental model behind coroutines.
questions.mistake: Calling coroutines lightweight threads without explaining suspension.
questions.followUp: When can a coroutine still block a thread?

questions.text: Which design patterns do you see in Android?
questions.answer: Builder (Retrofit, notifications), Observer (Flow, LiveData), Adapter (RecyclerView), Facade (repositories), Chain of responsibility (OkHttp interceptors), Factory (ViewModel factories), Singleton (Room via DI).
questions.why: They want patterns tied to real APIs.
questions.mistake: Reciting definitions with no Android example.
questions.followUp: Which pattern would you avoid overusing?

questions.text: Explain dependency inversion with an example.
questions.answer: The ViewModel depends on an `ArticleRepository` interface; the data layer implements it with Retrofit and Room; tests use a fake, and the network library can change without touching the ViewModel.
questions.why: It tests whether you can apply a principle rather than name it.
questions.mistake: Confusing the principle with using a DI library.
questions.followUp: Which other SOLID principle does this support?

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
data class User(val name: String)

val a = User("Sam")
val b = User("Sam")
println(a == b)
println(a === b)
quiz.explanation: == calls the generated equals(), so equal data matches. === checks whether both are the same object, and these are two instances.
quiz.why: It checks that you can tell equal values apart from the same instance, a frequent source of Java-to-Kotlin bugs.
quiz.mistake: Reading `==` as a reference check, as in Java. In Kotlin it calls `equals()`.

quiz.question: Which scope function uses this inside the lambda and returns the object itself?
quiz.explanation: apply exposes the object as this and returns it, which suits configuration. also returns the object too, but exposes it as it.
quiz.why: Picking the right scope function shows you read and write everyday Kotlin fluently.
quiz.mistake: Choosing `also` because it also returns the object. It passes the object as `it`, not `this`.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
val list = mutableListOf(1, 2)
list.add(3)
println(list.size)
quiz.explanation: val makes the reference read-only, not the object. The same mutable list is still changing, so its size is 3.
quiz.why: It tests whether you separate a read-only reference from an immutable object.
quiz.mistake: Believing `val` freezes the list. It only stops the variable from being reassigned.

quiz.question: Which builder returns a Deferred result?
quiz.explanation: async returns Deferred<T>, which you await(). launch returns a Job for side effects.
quiz.why: It confirms you know which builder to use when the caller needs a result back.
quiz.mistake: Picking `withContext`. It returns the value itself after suspending, not a `Deferred`.

quiz.question: A child fails inside supervisorScope. What happens to its siblings?
quiz.explanation: A supervisor isolates failures: one child failing does not cancel its siblings. In coroutineScope it would.
quiz.why: It checks that you can predict how far one failure spreads, which decides whether one bad request breaks a whole screen.
quiz.mistake: Thinking a supervisor also handles the exception. It protects siblings, but the failure still needs handling.

quiz.question: How do you move the upstream work of a flow to another dispatcher?
quiz.explanation: flowOn changes the upstream context. Emitting from another context inside flow {} breaks context preservation and throws.
quiz.why: It shows whether you know how to change threads in a flow without breaking its rules.
quiz.mistake: Wrapping `emit` in `withContext`, as you might in a suspend function. A `flow` builder throws if you do.

quiz.question: When must you not rely on onDestroy to save data?
options: Because the process can be killed without calling it
quiz.explanation: onDestroy is not guaranteed. Persist important data in onStop or as soon as it changes.
quiz.why: Interviewers want to know you won't lose user data by saving it too late.
quiz.mistake: Treating `onDestroy` as a guaranteed cleanup step. A killed process runs no more callbacks.

quiz.question: What can happen if you put a large object in the saved instance state Bundle?
quiz.explanation: The Bundle crosses Binder, whose buffer of about 1 MB is shared per process. Save IDs, not objects.
quiz.why: This crash tends to appear only with real data, so they check you know what belongs in saved state.
quiz.mistake: Treating the Bundle as general storage and saving whole lists or bitmaps in it.

quiz.question: What triggers recomposition of a scope?
options: A State read in that scope changing
Calling the composable from a ViewModel
quiz.explanation: Compose tracks State reads through the snapshot system and recomposes the scopes that read a changed value.
quiz.why: Almost every Compose performance and stale-screen bug comes back to this model.
quiz.mistake: Expecting a change to a plain variable to update the UI. Compose only tracks reads of snapshot state.

quiz.question: What does LaunchedEffect(userId) do when userId changes?
options: Runs a second coroutine alongside the first
Cancels the old coroutine and starts a new one
quiz.explanation: A changed key restarts the effect: the old coroutine is cancelled before the new one starts.
quiz.why: It checks that you understand how effect keys control a coroutine's lifetime.
quiz.mistake: Using a constant key such as `Unit` when the work depends on `userId`, so it never reloads.

quiz.question: Which keeps UI state across a configuration change?
quiz.explanation: rememberSaveable survives recomposition, configuration changes and process death. remember only survives recomposition.
quiz.why: Losing typed input on rotation is a visible bug, and they want to know you can prevent it.
quiz.mistake: Assuming `remember` survives rotation. It is lost when the Activity is recreated.

quiz.question: In an offline-first app, what does the UI read from?
quiz.explanation: The database is the single source of truth. The network only writes into it.
quiz.why: It tests whether you can design data flow that stays consistent with a poor or missing network.
quiz.mistake: Showing the network response directly and treating the database as a backup cache.

quiz.question: Where does a business rule reused by several screens belong?
quiz.explanation: A use case holds reusable business rules. A ViewModel manages screen state and UI events.
quiz.why: They want to see where you put logic so that it can be reused and tested.
quiz.mistake: Copying the rule into each ViewModel, where the copies drift apart.

quiz.question: What is @Binds used for?
options: Mapping an interface to its implementation
quiz.explanation: @Binds is an abstract declaration that maps an interface to an implementation. @Provides is factory code you write.
quiz.why: It shows whether you have written Hilt modules or only used ones that others wrote.
quiz.mistake: Putting `@Binds` on a function with a body. It must be abstract, and code you write needs `@Provides`.

quiz.question: Why prefer constructor injection over field injection?
options: It is the only kind Hilt supports
Dependencies are explicit and tests can build the object directly
It makes every object a singleton
quiz.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies visible, allows val fields and lets tests construct the class without the framework.
quiz.why: It checks that you see dependency injection as a design choice, not just a library.
quiz.mistake: Saying it is only shorter to write. The real gain is explicit dependencies and easy testing.

quiz.question: A Room Flow emits again although your result did not change. What helps?
quiz.explanation: Room re-emits on any change to the table. distinctUntilChanged() drops equal results; narrowing the query also helps.
quiz.why: It tests whether you know why observable queries can cause extra UI work.
quiz.mistake: Assuming Room emits only when your result changes. It re-runs the query when a table it reads changes.

quiz.question: Which is risky for tables holding user data?
quiz.explanation: A destructive fallback deletes data. Keep it for tables that are pure cache.
quiz.why: Deleting user data in an update is hard to undo, so they check how careful you are with schema changes.
quiz.mistake: Adding a destructive fallback to silence a migration crash, then shipping it.

quiz.question: What is the minimum interval for periodic WorkManager work?
quiz.explanation: Periodic work has a 15-minute minimum, and execution can drift.
quiz.why: It checks whether you know the platform limits before promising a sync schedule.
quiz.mistake: Planning to use periodic work for updates every minute. Shorter intervals are raised to 15 minutes.

quiz.question: What happens to scheduled WorkManager work after a user force-stops the app?
options: It runs once after a reboot
It does not run until the app is opened again
It moves to a foreground service
quiz.explanation: Force-stop clears scheduled jobs and alarms until the user opens the app again.
quiz.why: It helps explain "my sync stopped working" reports, and shows you know what the system won't let you do.
quiz.mistake: Claiming WorkManager always runs. After a force-stop, nothing runs until the app is started again.

quiz.question: What does a baseline profile do?
options: Gives AOT compile hints for critical code paths
quiz.explanation: It lets ART compile critical paths ahead of time, so early runs do not wait for JIT profiling.
quiz.why: It is a common startup improvement, and they want to know what it actually changes.
quiz.mistake: Describing it as a profiler or a size reducer. It tells ART which code to compile ahead of time.

quiz.question: Which can cause an ANR?
options: Blocking the main thread for about 5 s during input
A failed network call on a background thread
quiz.explanation: An input event with no response within about 5 s raises an ANR.
quiz.why: It checks that you know which work freezes the app and which only drops a frame.
quiz.mistake: Calling any slow frame an ANR. A slow frame is jank, while an ANR means the app stopped responding.

quiz.question: Which tool helps assert the values a Flow emits over time?
quiz.explanation: Turbine's test { awaitItem() } checks emissions one at a time inside runTest.
quiz.why: It shows whether you have tested streams that emit more than one value.
quiz.mistake: Checking only the first emission, so later wrong values go unnoticed.

quiz.question: What does Robolectric do?
options: Runs Android framework code on the JVM
quiz.explanation: Robolectric tests run on the JVM, so they are faster than instrumented tests on a device.
quiz.why: It tests whether you can choose the cheapest test that still gives enough confidence.
quiz.mistake: Treating a passing Robolectric test as proof that the feature works on real devices.

quiz.question: What best protects a third-party API secret your app needs?
options: Keep it on your backend and make the call there
quiz.explanation: Anything shipped in the app can be extracted. Moving the call behind your backend keeps the secret off the device.
quiz.why: They want to know you treat everything inside the APK as public.
quiz.mistake: Relying on obfuscation or encryption with a key in the app. An attacker can recover both.

quiz.question: What is the main operational risk of certificate pinning?
quiz.explanation: If a pinned certificate changes unexpectedly, the app cannot connect. Pin public keys and keep a backup pin.
quiz.why: It checks that you weigh a security gain against the risk of locking users out.
quiz.mistake: Pinning one certificate with no backup pin or recovery plan.

quiz.question: In Gradle, what does implementation do that api does not?
options: Keeps the dependency internal to the module
quiz.explanation: implementation keeps a dependency internal, so consumers need not recompile when it changes.
quiz.why: Dependency scope affects build speed and module boundaries in larger projects.
quiz.mistake: Using `api` everywhere so that things compile, which leaks dependencies and widens rebuilds.

quiz.question: Crashes appear during a staged rollout. What do you do first?
options: Wait a week for more data
quiz.explanation: Halt the rollout to limit impact, then triage, mitigate with a flag if possible and ship a tested fix.
quiz.why: It tests how you respond to a release incident under pressure.
quiz.mistake: Thinking a halt removes the update from people who have it. It only stops further distribution.

quiz.question: Why send an idempotency key with a chat message?
options: So a retry does not create a duplicate
quiz.explanation: On flaky networks a request may be retried. The key lets the server recognise it and not store the message twice.
quiz.why: Safe retries are central to any design that sends data over an unreliable network.
quiz.mistake: Preventing duplicates only by disabling the send button, which does nothing for automatic retries.

quiz.question: What is the type of `String::length` when passed to `map` on a `List<String>`?
quiz.explanation: An unbound member reference takes the receiver as its first parameter, so `String::length` is a `(String) -> Int`.
quiz.why: It checks that you can read function types, which appear throughout Kotlin APIs.
quiz.mistake: Picking `() -> Int` because `length` takes no argument, and forgetting the receiver must come from somewhere.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: Each call to makeCounter creates its own captured `count`. `a` has been called three times, so it returns 3; `b` is called once and returns 1.
quiz.why: It tests whether you understand what a lambda captures and how long that state lives.
quiz.mistake: Assuming all counters share one `count`, or that it resets on each call.

quiz.question: Inside a lambda of type `StringBuilder.() -> Unit`, what does `this` refer to?
quiz.explanation: In a function type with a receiver, the receiver becomes the implicit `this`, which is how `buildString` and `apply` let you call its members directly.
quiz.why: Receivers power Compose scopes and builder APIs, so they check you can follow what `this` means.
quiz.mistake: Reading `this` as the enclosing class. Inside the lambda, the receiver takes priority.

quiz.question: A Kotlin function `fun draw(label: String, width: Int = 1)` is called from Java. Without any annotation, which call compiles in Java?
quiz.explanation: Java can't use Kotlin default arguments, so it only sees the full signature. `@JvmOverloads` would generate `draw(String)` as well.
quiz.why: Mixed Java and Kotlin codebases make interop gaps a practical concern.
quiz.mistake: Expecting Java to use Kotlin default values. Without the annotation, Java must pass every argument.

quiz.question: Which Kotlin 2.2 feature lets a `when` branch read `is Failed if state.canRetry ->`?
quiz.explanation: Guard conditions, stable since Kotlin 2.2, let a branch of a `when` with a subject add an `if` condition.
quiz.why: It shows whether you keep up with language changes.
quiz.mistake: Confusing it with smart casts, which narrow the type but don't add a condition to a branch.

quiz.question: An exception is thrown inside the `collect { }` block below. What happens?
options: catch handles it and emits ErrorUi
The exception propagates to the collector's coroutine
quiz.explanation: `catch` only handles exceptions from upstream operators. `collect` is downstream, so the exception propagates. Move the work into `onEach` before `catch` to handle it.
quiz.why: It checks that you know where flow error handling stops.
quiz.mistake: Treating `.catch` as a try block around the whole chain, including `collect`.

quiz.question: Which operator should map each search query to a network request so that typing a new query cancels the previous request?
quiz.explanation: `flatMapLatest` cancels the previous inner flow whenever a new upstream value arrives.
quiz.why: It checks that you can match an operator to what should happen to work already running.
quiz.mistake: Using `flatMapConcat`, which makes every new query wait for the older ones to finish.

quiz.question: Which coroutine type is the closest replacement for RxJava's `BehaviorSubject`?
quiz.explanation: Like a BehaviorSubject, `MutableStateFlow` always holds a current value and gives it to new collectors.
quiz.why: Teams moving from RxJava need people who can map old types without changing behavior.
quiz.mistake: Treating it as an exact swap. `MutableStateFlow` needs an initial value and drops equal updates.

quiz.question: Which API tells you when the whole app moves to the background?
quiz.explanation: `ProcessLifecycleOwner` dispatches ON_STOP when the last activity stops and ON_START when the app returns. `Application.onTerminate` is never called on real devices.
quiz.why: Analytics, app locks and refresh logic often depend on knowing when the whole app leaves the screen.
quiz.mistake: Relying on one Activity's `onStop`, which also runs when you move to another screen in the app.

quiz.question: From which Android version must apps request a runtime permission before posting notifications?
quiz.explanation: `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` is a runtime permission for apps targeting Android 13 (API 33) and higher. Android 8.0 introduced notification channels.
quiz.why: It checks that you know the platform changes that affect whether users see your notifications.
quiz.mistake: Naming Android 8.0, which introduced notification channels, not the runtime permission.

quiz.question: Screen B returns a scanned QR code to screen A once. What is the recommended mechanism?
options: Passing a callback interface in the arguments Bundle
quiz.explanation: The Fragment Result API is designed for one-time results that fit in a Bundle. A shared ViewModel suits ongoing state.
quiz.why: It tests whether you can pass data between screens without tying them to each other.
quiz.mistake: Passing a callback between Fragments, which breaks when Android recreates them.

quiz.question: With Play App Signing, which certificate fingerprint belongs in `assetlinks.json` for production App Links?
options: The app signing key used by Play
Any key; the fingerprint isn't checked
quiz.explanation: Verification compares against the certificate that signs the installed app, which is Play's app signing key, not your upload key.
quiz.why: Links that work in testing but fail from the Play Store are a real release problem.
quiz.mistake: Listing only the upload key's fingerprint, so verification fails for installs from Play.

quiz.question: In `DiffUtil.ItemCallback`, what should `areItemsTheSame` compare?
options: A stable identity such as the item ID
quiz.explanation: `areItemsTheSame` asks whether two objects represent the same item, usually by ID. `areContentsTheSame` then checks whether its data changed.
quiz.why: Wrong diffing causes flicker and bad animations in lists, a part of many apps.
quiz.mistake: Comparing every field in `areItemsTheSame`, so an edited item looks like a new one.

quiz.question: Your app saves a photo it took into the user's gallery on Android 11+. Which permission does it need?
options: None when inserting your own media through MediaStore
quiz.explanation: Apps can add their own media through MediaStore without a permission. WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE has no effect for apps targeting Android 11+.
quiz.why: Asking for unneeded permissions hurts privacy and can cause Play policy problems.
quiz.mistake: Requesting broad storage access out of habit from older Android versions.

quiz.question: Which NetworkCallback method tells you that a connected network switched between metered and unmetered?
quiz.explanation: Capabilities such as NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_METERED can change while the network stays connected, and `onCapabilitiesChanged` reports it.
quiz.why: It shows whether your app can adapt large downloads to the user's connection.
quiz.mistake: Listening only for connect and disconnect, and missing changes on a network that stays connected.

quiz.question: Your SDK removes a deprecated public function. Under semantic versioning, which number goes up?
quiz.explanation: Removing public API is a breaking change, so it needs a MAJOR version bump.
quiz.why: Library and SDK users rely on version numbers to know whether an upgrade is safe.
quiz.mistake: Calling it a minor release because the function was deprecated first. Removing it can still break callers.

quiz.question: Why does an Android App Bundle usually give users a smaller download than a universal APK?
options: It is compressed with a better algorithm
Play serves only the code and resources each device needs
quiz.explanation: Play generates per-device APKs from the bundle, containing only that device's screen density, CPU architecture and languages.
quiz.why: It checks that you understand what happens between your build and the user's device.
quiz.mistake: Saying users install the bundle itself. Google Play builds APKs from it.

quiz.question: What is the correct way to show "1 item" or "5 items" in many languages?
quiz.explanation: Many languages have more plural forms than English, such as few or many. Plural resources let each translation define its own forms.
quiz.why: It tests whether you build for languages whose grammar differs from English.
quiz.mistake: Choosing between two strings with `count == 1`, which fails in languages with more plural forms.

quiz.question: Which call changes the app's language at runtime and also works below Android 13?
quiz.explanation: AppCompat 1.6+ `setApplicationLocales` supports per-app languages on Android 13+ and, with AppCompatActivity, on older versions. LocaleManager exists only on Android 13+.
quiz.why: Per-app language support has to work across old and new Android versions.
quiz.mistake: Changing the default locale or resources by hand, which is unreliable across configuration changes.

quiz.question: Two threads each call `count++` 1,000 times on `@Volatile var count = 0`. What is the final value?
quiz.explanation: `@Volatile` gives visibility, not atomicity. `count++` is read-modify-write, so updates can be lost. Use AtomicInteger or a lock.
quiz.why: It separates visibility from atomicity, the core of many threading bugs.
quiz.mistake: Believing `@Volatile` makes `count++` thread-safe.

quiz.question: When can an object reachable only through a WeakReference be collected?
options: Only when the app is closed
quiz.explanation: Weakly reachable objects can be collected at the next GC. Soft references are kept until memory is low.
quiz.why: It checks whether you know what a weak reference does before using one to fix a leak.
quiz.mistake: Expecting it to last until memory runs low, which is closer to how a `SoftReference` behaves.

quiz.question: Which design pattern do OkHttp interceptors implement?
quiz.explanation: Each interceptor handles the request and passes it along the chain with `chain.proceed()`, which is chain of responsibility.
quiz.why: They want to see that you recognize patterns in libraries you use, not only recite definitions.
quiz.mistake: Naming a pattern without explaining that each step can pass the request on, change it or answer it.

quiz.question: In double-checked locking for a singleton, why must the instance field be @Volatile?
options: So other threads never see a partly constructed object
quiz.explanation: Without volatile, the reference can be published before the constructor finishes. The volatile write creates the happens-before edge that prevents this.
quiz.why: It tests whether you understand safe publication, not just how to copy a singleton snippet.
quiz.mistake: Assuming `synchronized` is enough, although the first check reads the field outside the lock.

quiz.question: A Kotlin class has `companion object { fun create(): Foo }`. How does Java call it without any annotation?
quiz.explanation: The companion is compiled to a nested class with a static `Companion` field. Add `@JvmStatic` to allow `Foo.create()`.
quiz.why: It shows whether you know how Kotlin code looks to Java callers.
quiz.mistake: Assuming a companion function is a Java static. That needs `@JvmStatic`.

quiz.question: What does `x` hold?
quiz.code: val x = mutableListOf(1).also { it.add(2) }
quiz.explanation: `also` returns the object it was called on, not the lambda's result. The lambda added 2, so x is the list [1, 2]. With `let`, x would be `true`, the result of add.
quiz.why: Mixing up what scope functions return causes quiet bugs that still compile.
quiz.mistake: Expecting the lambda's result. `also` ignores it and returns the original object.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
val answer by lazy {
    print("init ")
    42
}
print("start ")
print("$answer ")
print("$answer")
quiz.explanation: A lazy value is computed on first access, not where it is declared, and only once.
quiz.why: It checks whether you know when delayed initialization actually runs.
quiz.mistake: Expecting the block to run where the property is declared, or again on every read.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
data class Cart(val items: MutableList<String>)

val first = Cart(mutableListOf("tea"))
val second = first.copy()
second.items.add("milk")
print(first.items.size)
quiz.explanation: copy() is shallow. Both carts hold the same list, so adding through one changes the other.
quiz.why: Shared mutable state hidden inside a copy is an easy bug to miss in UI state.
quiz.mistake: Assuming `copy()` also copies the objects that its properties refer to.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: equals() uses only primary-constructor properties, so the items are equal even though their quantities differ.
quiz.why: It tests whether you know which properties the generated data class methods use.
quiz.mistake: Expecting every property to count in `equals()`, including those declared in the class body.

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: m1 m2 m3 f10 f20 f30
m1 f10 m2 f20 m3 f30
quiz.explanation: A sequence processes one element through the whole chain, and first() stops after the first result.
quiz.why: It shows whether you understand lazy evaluation, not just that sequences exist.
quiz.mistake: Tracing it like a list, with all of `map` running before `filter` starts.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
open class Animal
class Dog : Animal()

fun Animal.sound() = "..."
fun Dog.sound() = "Woof"

val pet: Animal = Dog()
print(pet.sound())
quiz.explanation: Extensions are resolved from the declared type at compile time. The variable is declared as Animal.
quiz.why: It checks that you know extensions don't behave like overridden methods.
quiz.mistake: Expecting the object's runtime type to choose the extension.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: The base constructor runs first and calls the override before Child has set name, even though its type is non-null.
quiz.why: Calling overridable code during construction causes surprising nulls, even in null-safe Kotlin.
quiz.mistake: Trusting the non-null type. The subclass property hasn't been assigned yet.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: return@forEach leaves only the current lambda call, like continue in a loop.
quiz.why: A return inside a lambda is easy to misread in everyday code.
quiz.mistake: Treating `return@forEach` like `break`. The loop moves on to the next element.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: launch only schedules the child here. The parent prints B, yield() lets the child run, then C follows.
quiz.why: It tests whether you can trace what runs and when on a single thread.
quiz.mistake: Assuming `launch` runs its block immediately, before the next line.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: A failing async child cancels its coroutineScope even if await() is never called, and the scope rethrows the error.
quiz.why: Exception handling with `async` is where structured concurrency often surprises people.
quiz.mistake: Believing the exception stays inside the `Deferred` until someone calls `await()`.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: StateFlow does not emit a value equal to the current one, so setting 1 again does nothing.
quiz.why: It matters whenever an update seems to go missing from observed state.
quiz.mistake: Assuming every assignment emits, even when the new value equals the current one.

quiz.question: What is the bug?
options: delay() cannot be used inside try
catch (e: Exception) also catches CancellationException, so the loop keeps running after cancel()
quiz.explanation: Cancellation is delivered as an exception. Catching it lets the loop continue. Rethrow CancellationException or catch narrower types.
quiz.why: Broad catch blocks can quietly break cancellation in production code.
quiz.mistake: Assuming `cancel()` forces a coroutine to stop. Cancellation is cooperative and can be swallowed.

quiz.question: The collector never sees the new item. Why?
options: The list was changed in place, so StateFlow sees an equal value and emits nothing
quiz.explanation: Publish a new list instead: state.update { it + "new" }, with an immutable List type.
quiz.why: A screen that doesn't update is a common debugging task with `StateFlow`.
quiz.mistake: Reassigning the same list after changing it and expecting that to force an update.

quiz.question: Collecting this flow fails. Why?
options: trySend is not allowed in callbackFlow
The block ends without awaitClose, so callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException
quiz.explanation: callbackFlow requires awaitClose, which keeps the flow open and is where you unregister the listener.
quiz.why: Wrapping callback APIs is common, and cleanup is the part that causes leaks.
quiz.mistake: Ending the block after registering the callback, with nothing to keep the flow open or unregister it.

quiz.question: Collecting this flow throws. Why?
options: emit is not a suspend function
A flow builder must not emit from another context; use flowOn
Dispatchers.Default cannot be used in runBlocking
quiz.explanation: Flows preserve context. Change where upstream code runs with flowOn instead of switching around emit.
quiz.why: It checks that you know the threading rule behind `flow`, not only the operator names.
quiz.mistake: Assuming a `flow` builder allows the same context switches as any suspend function.

quiz.question: This prints false. What is the bug?
quiz.code:
data class User(var name: String)

val user = User("Sam")
val online = hashSetOf(user)
user.name = "Alex"
print(user in online)
options: The var used by hashCode changed after insertion, so the set looks in the wrong bucket
Data classes cannot be stored in sets
quiz.explanation: Never change a property used by equals() or hashCode() while the object is a key or set element. Prefer val and copy().
quiz.why: It tests whether you understand how hash-based collections find objects.
quiz.mistake: Assuming a set rechecks every element. It first looks in the bucket for the current hash.

quiz.question: What is wrong with this Fragment code?
options: collect must be called from onCreate
It uses the Fragment lifecycle and never pauses, so it can update a destroyed view and keeps working in the background
StateFlow cannot be collected in a Fragment
quiz.explanation: Use viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope with repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED).
quiz.why: Lifecycle-unsafe collection can cause crashes and wasted work that are hard to trace.
quiz.mistake: Thinking `lifecycleScope` alone is safe. It cancels only when the Fragment is destroyed and doesn't pause in the background.

quiz.question: The counter stays at 0 on screen. Why?
options: The state is not remembered, so each recomposition creates a new one starting at 0
quiz.explanation: Wrap it in remember, or rememberSaveable to also keep it across rotation.
quiz.why: It is a quick check that you understand how composables keep state.
quiz.mistake: Thinking `mutableStateOf` keeps its value by itself. It must also be remembered.

quiz.question: What is the bug?
options: lateinit cannot be used in an object
A process-wide object keeps the Activity, so it can never be garbage collected
An Activity is not a Context
quiz.explanation: Store activity.applicationContext, or pass a Context only when needed.
quiz.why: Context leaks are a classic Android memory problem, and they check you can spot one in review.
quiz.mistake: Thinking `private` or `lateinit` prevents the leak. What matters is how long the reference lives.

quiz.question: Selecting a different user does not reload the profile. Why?
options: Unit never changes, so LaunchedEffect only runs on initial composition and ignores new userId values
quiz.explanation: LaunchedEffect restarts only when one of its keys changes. Pass userId as the key: LaunchedEffect(userId).
quiz.why: Stale effects when navigation arguments or IDs change are a frequent Compose bug.
quiz.mistake: Using LaunchedEffect(Unit) out of habit when the effect actually depends on a parameter.

quiz.question: When the top item is removed, the wrong row stays expanded. Why?
options: Without a stable key, remembered state stays tied to the list index rather than the item ID
quiz.explanation: By default, LazyColumn keys items by their index. Pass key = { it.id } so remembered state moves with the item, or hoist expanded state.
quiz.why: It tests whether you understand how Compose matches remembered slots to list items.
quiz.mistake: Omitting keys in LazyColumn and assuming Compose tracks items by object equality.

quiz.question: The user scrolls 300 pixels down without crossing item 0. How many times does the Text recompose?
options: Zero times, because the boolean result of derivedStateOf stayed false
quiz.explanation: derivedStateOf only notifies readers when its computed result changes. Since firstVisibleItemIndex stayed 0, showTop stayed false and nothing recomposed.
quiz.why: It checks that you know how derivedStateOf reduces recompositions on fast-changing state.
quiz.mistake: Thinking derivedStateOf recomposes whenever any input inside the block changes.

quiz.question: Creating two instances of SettingsRepo crashes at runtime. Why?
options: Each SettingsRepo creates a new DataStore delegate for the same file, which throws IllegalStateException
Context cannot be passed to a repository
quiz.explanation: DataStore enforces one instance per file per process. Declare the preferencesDataStore delegate at the top level or provide it as a @Singleton.
quiz.why: Multiple DataStore instances for one file are a classic crash when teams forget singleton scoping.
quiz.mistake: Putting the preferencesDataStore property delegate inside a class instead of at top-level.

quiz.question: When the server keeps returning 401, what happens with this OkHttp Authenticator?
options: OkHttp stops automatically after one retry
It retries 401 responses in a loop until OkHttp hits its internal follow-up limit
quiz.explanation: Without checking response.priorResponse != null (or counting prior responses), authenticate() keeps retrying on repeated 401s. Return null when already retried or when refresh fails.
quiz.why: Unbounded 401 retries hammer the auth server and stall user requests.
quiz.mistake: Returning a new Request unconditionally without checking priorResponse.

quiz.question: What happens when Hilt compiles this class?
options: Hilt injects the Application context instead
The build fails because a @Singleton cannot depend on an @ActivityContext
It compiles and leaks the first Activity
quiz.explanation: SingletonComponent outlives ActivityComponent, so Hilt rejects injecting @ActivityContext into a @Singleton at compile time. Use @ApplicationContext.
quiz.why: Understanding Hilt component lifetimes prevents both compile errors and context leaks.
quiz.mistake: Using @ActivityContext anywhere a Context is needed instead of @ApplicationContext for long-lived objects.

quiz.question: Opening the screen five times queues five identical upload jobs. Why?
options: enqueue() always adds a new request; use enqueueUniqueWork with ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP or REPLACE
WorkManager requires a tag to deduplicate
quiz.explanation: Every enqueue() call schedules a separate WorkRequest. Use enqueueUniqueWork("sync", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, req) to avoid duplicate work.
quiz.why: Duplicate background jobs waste battery, data, and server capacity.
quiz.mistake: Calling enqueue() from lifecycle callbacks or screen opens without a unique work name.

quiz.question: This JVM unit test crashes before checking uiState. Why?
options: viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main, which is not set in a plain JVM unit test without Dispatchers.setMain
quiz.explanation: Android's Main looper does not exist on the JVM. Install a TestDispatcher with Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher) in @Before or a MainDispatcherRule.
quiz.why: Testing ViewModels on the JVM is a daily task, and Main dispatcher setup is the first hurdle.
quiz.mistake: Assuming runTest replaces Dispatchers.Main automatically.

quiz.question: What is the security flaw in this biometric unlock?
options: BiometricPrompt cannot run on the main thread
Without a CryptoObject backed by a Keystore key, a hooking tool on a rooted device can invoke onAuthenticationSucceeded directly
AuthenticationResult must be persisted in SharedPreferences
quiz.explanation: Always pass a Cipher from an auth-bound Android Keystore key as a CryptoObject and decrypt the secret inside onAuthenticationSucceeded.
quiz.why: It separates UI-only biometric checks from hardware-enforced authentication.
quiz.mistake: Treating the success callback as sufficient proof when protecting sensitive local data.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.code:
val a = "hi"
val b = "hi"
val c = String(charArrayOf('h', 'i'))
println("${a === b} ${a === c}")
quiz.explanation: String literals "hi" are interned in the JVM string pool, so a and b point to the same object (true). Constructing a String from a CharArray allocates a new object on the heap (false).
quiz.why: It tests whether you understand JVM string interning and reference equality.
quiz.mistake: Expecting both to be true because they hold the same characters, or confusing === with ==.

quiz.question: A tablet user opens the app in split-screen and the two-pane layout clips awkwardly. Why?
options: LocalConfiguration cannot be read in Compose
smallestScreenWidthDp reflects the physical display, not the app's current window size in split-screen or multi-window mode
600 dp is only for landscape phones
quiz.explanation: Use currentWindowAdaptiveInfo().windowSizeClass, which reflects the actual window width so split-screen and foldables adapt dynamically.
quiz.why: Adaptive layouts break on tablets and foldables when developers check hardware traits instead of window size.
quiz.mistake: Using smallestScreenWidthDp or an isTablet boolean instead of WindowSizeClass.

quiz.question: Users are locked out of the app when the server renews its TLS certificate. Why?
quiz.code:
val pinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/CURRENT_LEAF_CERT_ONLY=")
    .build()
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder().certificatePinner(pinner).build()
options: Only one pin is configured with no backup key, so rotating the certificate breaks all installed clients
sha256 pins are ignored on Android 13+
quiz.explanation: Always pin the SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) hash and include at least one backup pin (plus an expiration or remote kill switch) so rotation doesn't cause an outage.
quiz.why: Pinning without a rotation plan is the most common real-world SSL pinning outage.
quiz.mistake: Pinning a single leaf certificate without a backup pin.

quiz.question: What is the security risk in this deep-link WebView?
options: An attacker can pass an arbitrary URL in the deep link and call AuthBridge methods from JavaScript
quiz.explanation: Never load unvalidated URLs from deep links, and never expose a @JavascriptInterface to untrusted origins. Allow-list exact hosts/schemes or use a Custom Tab.
quiz.why: Combining an unvalidated URL with a JS bridge exposes native app capabilities to untrusted web pages.
quiz.mistake: Trusting query parameters in a deep link without host and scheme validation.

quiz.question: What does this print in Kotlin 2.2+?
quiz.explanation: Non-local break and continue inside inline lambdas became stable in Kotlin 2.2. When it == 2, continue jumps to the next iteration of the outer for-loop (3, 4).
quiz.why: It tests whether you know how Kotlin 2.2+ non-local continue behaves across an outer loop.
quiz.mistake: Confusing continue (which skips the rest of the outer loop iteration) with return@forEach.

quiz.question: Why does get(1) fail to prevent key 1 from being evicted?
options: The third constructor argument is false (insertion order), so get() does not move the entry to most-recently-used
quiz.explanation: Pass accessOrder = true as the third argument to LinkedHashMap so reads via get() also update recency.
quiz.why: An LRU cache that only orders by insertion behaves like a FIFO queue, not LRU.
quiz.mistake: Forgetting the accessOrder = true flag on LinkedHashMap.

quiz.question: Which API generates a Material 3 color scheme from the user's wallpaper on Android 12+?
quiz.explanation: On API 31+ (Android 12+), dynamicLightColorScheme(context) and dynamicDarkColorScheme(context) read the system wallpaper palette.
quiz.why: Material 3 dynamic color is part of Google's Compose training and modern Android UI design.
quiz.mistake: Calling dynamic color APIs without checking Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.S.

quiz.question: Why does onNodeWithText("Badge") fail to find the inner Text here?
options: Text cannot be inside a Row
Descendants are merged into one node, so querying a single child requires useUnmergedTree = true
quiz.explanation: When descendants are merged, the combined node holds the merged text. Pass useUnmergedTree = true to inspect individual child nodes.
quiz.why: Compose UI tests and TalkBack share the same merged vs. unmerged semantics tree.
quiz.mistake: Adding redundant testTags instead of understanding merged semantics.

quiz.question: When should you use a plain @Stable state-holder class instead of a ViewModel?
options: When fetching data from Room or Retrofit
For reusable UI-element logic like scroll, focus, or expand/collapse with no business dependencies
Whenever you want state to survive process death automatically
quiz.explanation: Plain state holders manage UI-element state and UI logic inside composition via remember; ViewModels manage screen-level state and data-layer access.
quiz.why: Google's app architecture guide separates screen-level ViewModels from UI-element state holders.
quiz.mistake: Pushing pure visual state like tooltip or drawer animation flags into a ViewModel.

quiz.question: Which Compose test rule tests a stateless composable without launching an Activity?
quiz.explanation: createComposeRule() hosts your composable in an empty test container, which is faster and simpler for stateless UI components.
quiz.why: Stateless composables let you test UI rendering and callbacks in isolation.
quiz.mistake: Launching MainActivity with Hilt for every small component test.

quiz.question: Which capability does an abstract class have in Kotlin that an interface does not?
options: Constructors and backing fields for state
quiz.explanation: Kotlin interfaces can have default methods and abstract properties, but cannot have constructors or store state in backing fields.
quiz.why: It tests whether you know the real boundary between interfaces and abstract classes in Kotlin.
quiz.mistake: Saying interfaces cannot have method implementations, as in older Java.

quiz.question: A user taps a notification to open DetailActivity and presses Back, but the app exits instead of going to MainActivity. What fixes this?
options: Build the PendingIntent with TaskStackBuilder and parentActivityName
quiz.explanation: TaskStackBuilder constructs a synthetic back stack from the manifest parent hierarchy so navigating back from a notification goes to MainActivity.
quiz.why: Notification entry points often feel broken if Back exits the app immediately.
quiz.mistake: Creating a PendingIntent with a single Activity Intent when the user expects parent navigation.

quiz.question: What happens when you chain WorkManager requests with beginWith(compress).then(upload).enqueue()?
options: upload runs only after compress succeeds, and receives compress's output Data as its input
upload runs even if compress fails
quiz.explanation: Chained work runs sequentially: if compress fails or is cancelled, upload never runs; if compress succeeds, its output Data merges into upload's inputData.
quiz.why: Multi-step background pipelines (e.g. compress then upload) rely on WorkManager chaining.
quiz.mistake: Enqueueing both requests independently and assuming they will run in order.
